clue.text: Dry spell's very onerous in limits of desert

indicators.note: in tells us the next piece sits inside the outer letters
the limits of a word are its first and last letters, here of desert

parts.note: a very onerous time is a rough one

explanation.surface: A drought is described as especially hard going in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'limits of desert' gives D and T, and 'in' puts ROUGH between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A long period without rain is a dry spell.

clue.text: Endlessly crude chap upset? Upset

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means the pieces are turned upside down, read bottom to top
endlessly says the word for crude loses its final letter

parts.note: a crude, coarse person is a brute
Sid is a common man's name, standing for any chap

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a rough fellow is upset, and answers yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' trims BRUTE to BRUT; add SID and 'upset' turns BRUTSID round. The first 'upset' is the reversal signal, the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To disturb someone is to upset or agitate them.

clue.text: Dismissed person's appearance possibly in prospect

parts.note: a batsman dismissed in cricket is out
a person's appearance is their look

explanation.surface: A rejected candidate's looks might count for something in their prospects.
explanation.definitionFit: Outlook and prospect both mean the view of what lies ahead.

clue.text: Snatch idiot away from grass snake

indicators.note: away from tells us one piece is taken out of the others

parts.note: taken as written
an ass is a fool
an asp is a venomous snake

explanation.surface: Someone foolish is told to grab a grass snake.
explanation.walkthrough: GRASS + ASP gives GRASSASP; removing ASS leaves GR + ASP.
explanation.definitionFit: To snatch something is to seize or grip it quickly.

clue.text: Scientific instrument with wrought steel covering

indicators.note: wrought means worked or shaped, so the letters of steel are reworked

parts.note: a cope is a long cloak worn by clergy, a covering

explanation.surface: A lab device is housed in a casing of worked steel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrought' rearranges STEEL into TELES, then COPE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A telescope is an optical device used by astronomers and other scientists.

clue.text: Pay for your own energy from a European source

parts.note: go means energy or vigour, as in full of go
Dutch means coming from the Netherlands, a European country

explanation.surface: Paying your own way is presented as power drawn from a European supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: Going Dutch means each diner settles their own share.
explanation.definitionFit: To go Dutch is the idiom for each person paying their share of a bill.

clue.text: As seen in onset of Gold Rush?

definitions.text: As seen in onset of Gold Rush?

indicators.note: the onset of a word is its first letter, here of Gold

parts.note: a rush is a reed-like waterside plant

explanation.surface: The clue asks whether avarice is what drove the start of a gold rush.
explanation.walkthrough: G from 'onset of Gold' plus REED, a rush; the whole clue also describes the avarice of prospectors.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice for wealth is exactly what powered the prospectors of a gold rush.

clue.text: Chapter I'd rewritten, at little expense

indicators.note: rewritten means the letters of chapter and I'd are written again in a new order

explanation.surface: An author redrafts a chapter cheaply.
explanation.definitionFit: Something very cheap costs very little, the sense of this compound.

clue.text: City I encountered with journey round capital of Libya?

parts.note: a trip is a journey
O is round in shape

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter, here of Libya

explanation.surface: A traveller meets a city on a trip around the Libyan capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I encountered with' sets I beside the other pieces at the end. The question mark is because the city named is indeed the capital of Libya.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is a city, the capital of Libya.

clue.text: It's presumably costly, given 6

parts.note: 6 is the phrase meaning very inexpensive; read literally, if dirt is that cheap, cleanliness must be the expensive thing

explanation.surface: A price comparison: one thing must be dear if its opposite costs nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 6-down's phrase is taken literally: if dirt is cheap, its opposite, cleanliness, must cost a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Hygiene is cleanliness, the opposite of dirt.

clue.text: Leave stage displays to look bad

parts.note: stage sets are the scenery on display in a theatre
to ail is to be unwell, looking poorly

explanation.surface: Advice to quit a theatre whose scenery looks shabby.
explanation.walkthrough: Set sail is to leave port; SETS + AIL splits it differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To set sail is to depart by ship, to leave.

clue.text: Mistaken about a piece of jewellery

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the word for mistaken goes round a

parts.note: erring means going wrong, mistaken

explanation.surface: Someone is wrong about an item of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: ERRING goes about A: E(A)RRING.
explanation.definitionFit: An earring is an ornament worn on the ear, a jewellery item.

clue.text: Naturally observed to embrace work done without rival

indicators.note: to embrace means to hold inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a subject observed naturally is unposed, not arranged for the camera
op is short for opus, a work completed

explanation.surface: A natural observer takes on a job with no competition.
explanation.walkthrough: OP goes inside UNPOSED after UN.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate standing unopposed has no rival.

clue.text: Hard to block fuel — it helps start the car

indicators.note: to block means to obstruct by sitting inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: coke is a fuel made from coal
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A motoring tip about blocking the fuel supply when starting a car.
explanation.walkthrough: H goes inside COKE. A choke, which restricts air to enrich the fuel mixture, was used to start older cars from cold.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's choke valve aided cold starts by richening the fuel mixture.

clue.text: of Charlie?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is 'of Charlie?' (5): the opening words are lost in the OCR, no scan is supplied and a search for the clue text found no other print, so the definition and wordplay cannot be shown.

clue.text: Soldiers, abusive, not allowed in as a consequence

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a body of soldiers

indicators.note: not allowed means the following word is kept out of the word for abusive

parts.note: abusive remarks are insulting

explanation.surface: Soldiers barred entry after being rude, as a consequence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in not allowed' removes IN from INSULTING, leaving SULTING after RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something following as a consequence is the resulting outcome.

clue.text: Like the job of railwayman leaving leaves here?

definitions.text: Like the job of railwayman leaving leaves here?

parts.words: Like the job of railwayman leaving leaves here?
parts.note: a job at risk is said to be in jeopardy; a railwayman who left fallen leaves on the track, the classic British rail delay excuse, would be in that state

explanation.surface: A rail worker who lets autumn leaves stay on the track is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves on the line' is the notorious British railway excuse for autumn delays; the phrase also means at risk, as a careless worker's job would be.
explanation.definitionFit: A job in jeopardy is at stake, and the track is where leaves cause delays.

clue.text: Accepting different attitude to cleaner, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that to cleaner may be read as another word once its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cleaner is perhaps met with an open-minded outlook.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerance is an outlook that accepts views or ways unlike one's own.

clue.text: No time for position to have an effect in Cornish town

indicators.note: no means the following letter is taken out of the word for position

parts.note: status is one's position or standing
to tell is to have a marked effect, as in 'the strain began to tell'

explanation.surface: A Cornish town where a lack of time makes rank count.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing a T from STATUS leaves STAUS, then TELL. St Austell is a town in Cornwall, the county at England's south-west tip.
explanation.definitionFit: St Austell is a market town in Cornwall, a county in south-west England.

clue.text: Criticised about note being biased

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the word for criticised goes round note

parts.note: to be slated is to be harshly criticised
N, for north, is a compass point; here a common crossword note

explanation.surface: A partial report is criticised for a remark about bias.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside SLATED: SLA(N)TED.
explanation.definitionFit: A slanted account leans one way, so it is partial.

clue.text: 22 coming round about clothing

indicators.note: coming round means encircling, so the answer to 22 goes round the next piece

parts.note: 22-across is the word meaning shock or horrify
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A shocking garment is discussed.
explanation.walkthrough: RE goes inside the 22-across answer: APPA(RE)L.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparel is a formal word for clothes and garments.

clue.text: Post Office dog appearing on opening?

parts.note: a pup is a young dog

explanation.surface: A puppy turns up at the post office opening.
explanation.walkthrough: A pop-up book or window appears when it is opened.
explanation.definitionFit: A pop-up card or advert springs into view when opened.

clue.text: Comedian's lines — new, but exhibiting a recognisable feature

parts.note: patter is the fast stream of talk in a comic's act

explanation.surface: A comic's routine is fresh yet still has a recognisable signature.
explanation.definitionFit: A pattern is a repeated, recognisable design or trait.

clue.text: Seaside feature: rubbish entertainer!

parts.note: a pier is a structure jutting into the sea at a resort
rot means nonsense, rubbish

explanation.surface: Someone pans a seaside show as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: A pierrot is a clown in a white costume, once a stock seaside-resort entertainer in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierrots were costumed clown performers who sang at British seaside resorts.

clue.text: Shock: earthquake initially omitted from charity campaign

indicators.note: omitted from means a letter is dropped out of the word that follows

parts.note: a charity appeal is a fundraising campaign

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter of earthquake

explanation.surface: A disaster fund drive leaves out the earthquake, causing shock.
explanation.walkthrough: E, the first letter of 'earthquake', is dropped from APPEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal someone is to horrify or dismay them.

clue.text: Balletic movement from dancing troupe — it's ultimate in finesse

indicators.note: dancing means the letters of troupe and it move about into a new order

parts.note: the 's is the verb has, linking it to the next piece

indicators.note: the ultimate in a word is its last letter, here of finesse

explanation.surface: A dance company performs a ballet move with the utmost grace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' rearranges TROUPE + IT into PIROUETT, then 'ultimate in finesse' adds E.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirouette is a full spin on one foot in ballet.

clue.text: Fold last of oil into another fuel

indicators.note: into means the letter goes inside the other piece

parts.note: peat is a fuel cut from bogs

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, here of oil

explanation.surface: Fuel types are mixed in an instruction about folding.
explanation.walkthrough: L, the last letter of 'oil', goes inside PEAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is a fold pressed into fabric.

clue.text: Still one university crazy to incorporate college

indicators.note: to incorporate means to take inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a nut is a crazy person

explanation.surface: A university oddball takes in a college while still whole.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes inside NUT, after U. 'Still one' means still in one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left intact, in one piece, has not been sliced.

clue.text: Insect: call it the ultimate in pestilence

parts.note: to term something is to call or name it

indicators.note: the ultimate in a word is its last letter, here of pestilence

explanation.surface: An insect is branded the worst sort of pest.
explanation.definitionFit: Termites are wood-eating social insects.

clue.text: Little change to obscure form of power

indicators.note: little change says the word for obscure is altered only slightly, one letter shifting place

parts.note: something obscure is unclear

explanation.surface: A small adjustment to a murky energy source.
explanation.walkthrough: In UNCLEAR the U moves one place, after the N.
explanation.definitionFit: Atomic energy is one form of power generation.

clue.text: side of pleasure

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is 'side of pleasure' (7): the opening is lost in the OCR, no scan is supplied and a search for the clue text found no other print, so the wordplay cannot be shown.

clue.text: Included in edited text and no longer seen

indicators.note: in means the first piece is placed inside the second
edited means the letters of text are rearranged

parts.note: Inc, short for incorporated, means included as part of a body

explanation.surface: A passage was included in an edited text and vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edited' turns TEXT into EXTT; INC goes in after EXT.
explanation.definitionFit: An extinct species has died out, so it is not seen any more.
